topic: GROUP BY and HAVING in SQL

questions.question: What is the GROUP BY clause in SQL and how does it work?
questions.title: GROUP BY Clause in SQL
questions.direct_answer: **GROUP BY** collapses rows that share the same value(s) into groups, so aggregates (`COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`) produce **one result per group**. Every column in the SELECT must be either inside an aggregate or listed in `GROUP BY`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand GROUP BY buckets rows and the SELECT-column rule.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Selecting a non-aggregated column that isn't in GROUP BY.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that GROUP BY runs after WHERE and before HAVING/SELECT.

sections.title: How GROUP BY Works
sections.content:
**`GROUP BY`** buckets rows that share the same value in one or more columns, then an aggregate computes a single value for each bucket. `GROUP BY department` with `COUNT(*)` gives the headcount **per department** — one row per department.

The rule that catches everyone: every column in `SELECT` must be either **wrapped in an aggregate** or **listed in GROUP BY**. Otherwise the database can't decide which row's value to show for that group.

sections.title: GROUP BY at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~buckets rows|by shared column values|one row per group|enables per-group aggregates
emerald|SELECT rule|~aggregate or grouped|column in GROUP BY|or inside COUNT/SUM|else error
amber|Order|~runs mid-query|after WHERE|before HAVING/SELECT|filter rows first
rose|Multi-column|~finer buckets|GROUP BY a, b|one row per (a,b) pair|order doesn't change result

sections.title: Count per group
sections.content:
```sql
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount, AVG(salary) AS avg_pay
FROM employees
GROUP BY department;
```

Sample output:

| department | headcount | avg_pay |
|---|---|---|
| Tech | 12 | 95000 |
| Sales | 7 | 60000 |
| Finance | 4 | 88000 |

*One summary row per department.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Ungrouped column in SELECT**: `SELECT name, department, COUNT(*) GROUP BY department` fails — `name` is neither grouped nor aggregated.
- **Filtering groups in WHERE**: aggregate conditions go in HAVING.
- **Expecting order**: GROUP BY doesn't sort — add ORDER BY if you need it.
- **Grouping by a column you don't need**: extra GROUP BY columns split buckets finer than intended.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **GROUP BY** buckets rows by shared values.
- **One result row per group** after aggregation.
- **Every SELECT column** must be aggregated or in GROUP BY.
- **Runs after WHERE**, before HAVING and SELECT.
- **Doesn't sort** — add ORDER BY for ordered output.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: GROUP BY takes rows that share the same value in one or more columns and collapses them into groups, so that an aggregate function produces one result per group instead of one for the whole table. So GROUP BY department with COUNT star gives me the headcount for each department, one row per department, and I can add AVG of salary to get the average pay per department in the same query. The rule that trips up almost every beginner is the SELECT column rule: every column you put in the SELECT list must either be wrapped in an aggregate function or appear in the GROUP BY clause. The reason is that each output row represents a whole group, so if you select a column like employee name that isn't grouped or aggregated, the database has no way to know which name to show for that group, and it rejects the query. It also helps to know where GROUP BY sits in execution: it runs after WHERE, so you filter individual rows first, and before HAVING and SELECT, so HAVING can then filter the groups. One more practical note: GROUP BY does not sort the output, so if you want the departments in a particular order you have to add an explicit ORDER BY.

Does GROUP BY sort the results?

questions.question: What is the HAVING clause in SQL and when do you use it?
questions.title: HAVING Clause in SQL — Filtering Groups
questions.direct_answer: **HAVING** filters **groups** after `GROUP BY`, using aggregate conditions like `COUNT(*) > 5`. It's the group-level counterpart to `WHERE` (which filters rows before grouping). You use HAVING precisely when the condition depends on an aggregated value.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know HAVING filters groups using aggregates after GROUP BY.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting aggregate conditions in WHERE, or row conditions in HAVING.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note WHERE filters before grouping (faster), HAVING after — prefer WHERE when possible.

sections.title: What HAVING Does
sections.content:
**`HAVING`** applies a filter to **groups** produced by `GROUP BY`, and it's the only clause where an aggregate condition like `COUNT(*) > 5` or `SUM(total) > 10000` is legal. `WHERE` can't do this because it runs *before* grouping, when aggregates don't yet exist.

Think of it as a two-stage filter: `WHERE` trims rows going *into* the groups, `HAVING` trims the groups *coming out*. Prefer WHERE for any non-aggregate condition because it filters earlier and faster.

sections.title: HAVING at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~filters groups|after GROUP BY|aggregate conditions OK|COUNT(*) > 5
emerald|vs WHERE|~stage difference|WHERE filters rows first|HAVING filters groups after|both can appear
amber|Performance|~filter early|WHERE shrinks input|HAVING runs on grouped data|prefer WHERE
rose|Rule|~by condition type|row value -> WHERE|aggregate value -> HAVING|

sections.title: WHERE + GROUP BY + HAVING together
sections.content:
```sql
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM employees
WHERE active = true          -- row filter first
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5          -- keep only big departments
ORDER BY headcount DESC;
```

Sample output:

| department | headcount |
|---|---|
| Tech | 12 |
| Sales | 7 |

*Active employees grouped by department, keeping only departments with more than five.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Aggregate in WHERE**: `WHERE COUNT(*) > 5` is illegal — use HAVING.
- **Row filter in HAVING**: works but is slower; put it in WHERE.
- **HAVING without GROUP BY**: legal in some DBs (treats whole table as one group), but usually a mistake.
- **Using a SELECT alias in HAVING**: portability varies — repeat the aggregate to be safe.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **HAVING** filters groups after GROUP BY.
- **Only place** an aggregate condition is legal.
- **WHERE** filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after.
- **Prefer WHERE** for non-aggregate conditions (faster).
- **Common pattern**: WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: HAVING is the clause you use to filter groups after a GROUP BY, and it's the only place where an aggregate condition like COUNT greater than five or SUM of total greater than ten thousand is allowed. The reason WHERE can't do this is timing: WHERE runs before grouping happens, so at that point the aggregates don't exist yet. HAVING runs after the groups are formed, so it can look at each group's count or sum and decide whether to keep it. I think of it as a two-stage filter. WHERE trims the individual rows that go into the groups, and HAVING trims the groups that come back out. A typical query uses both: I might write WHERE active equals true to consider only active employees, then GROUP BY department, then HAVING COUNT greater than five to keep only the larger departments. The performance tip that makes you stand out is to always push non-aggregate conditions into WHERE rather than HAVING, because WHERE filters earlier and reduces how many rows have to be grouped, which is faster. So the simple rule is: if your condition is about a raw row value, it goes in WHERE; if it's about an aggregated value for the whole group, it goes in HAVING.

questions.question: How do you group by multiple columns in SQL?
questions.title: Grouping by Multiple Columns in SQL
questions.direct_answer: **Grouping by multiple columns** (`GROUP BY a, b`) creates one group per **unique combination** of those columns' values — finer buckets than a single column. The column order in GROUP BY doesn't change the result, only how you read it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know multi-column GROUP BY groups by value combinations.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Expecting GROUP BY a, b to behave like grouping by a alone.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note that all non-aggregated SELECT columns must appear in the multi-column GROUP BY.

sections.title: Grouping by Multiple Columns
sections.content:
**`GROUP BY a, b`** forms one group for every distinct **combination** of `a` and `b`. Grouping sales by `region, product` gives one row per region-and-product pair — more granular than grouping by region alone.

The order of columns in `GROUP BY` doesn't affect *which* groups exist (the combinations are the same); it only affects readability. As always, every non-aggregated SELECT column must appear in the GROUP BY list.

sections.title: Multi-Column GROUP BY at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~groups by combination|one row per (a,b)|finer than single column|distinct pairs
emerald|Order|~doesn't change groups|GROUP BY a,b = b,a|same buckets|affects readability only
amber|SELECT rule|~all grouped cols allowed|every non-agg col in GROUP BY|aggregates summarize|
rose|Use|~cross-tab style|region x product|year x month|category breakdowns

sections.title: Group by two columns
sections.content:
```sql
SELECT region, product, SUM(amount) AS sales
FROM orders
GROUP BY region, product
ORDER BY region, sales DESC;
```

Sample output:

| region | product | sales |
|---|---|---|
| East | Phone | 9000 |
| East | Cable | 1200 |
| West | Phone | 7000 |

*One row per region-and-product combination.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting single-column behaviour**: `GROUP BY region, product` splits each region into per-product rows.
- **Missing a SELECT column in GROUP BY**: every non-aggregated column must be listed.
- **Assuming column order matters**: it changes display logic, not the groups.
- **Too many GROUP BY columns**: over-splitting yields tiny, less useful groups.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`GROUP BY a, b`** = one group per unique (a, b) combination.
- **Finer granularity** than grouping by one column.
- **Order of GROUP BY columns** doesn't change the groups.
- **All non-aggregated SELECT columns** must be in GROUP BY.
- **Great for** cross-tab style breakdowns.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Grouping by multiple columns means you list more than one column after GROUP BY, and SQL then creates one group for every distinct combination of those columns' values. So if I group sales by region and product, I get one row per region-and-product pair, which is finer-grained than grouping by region alone. With region alone I'd get one row per region; with region and product I get, say, East phones, East cables, West phones, and so on. This is exactly what you want for breakdowns or cross-tab style reports, like sales by year and month, or counts by category and status. A couple of details. The order in which you list the columns in GROUP BY does not change which groups are formed, because the set of distinct combinations is the same either way; it mainly affects how you read or sort the output, and I usually pair it with an ORDER BY on the same columns for a clean layout. And the SELECT column rule still applies and is even more important here: every non-aggregated column in your SELECT must appear in the GROUP BY list. The thing to avoid is over-splitting; if you group by too many columns you can end up with lots of tiny groups that aren't very meaningful.

questions.question: What is the SQL execution order for GROUP BY queries?
questions.title: SQL Execution Order with GROUP BY and HAVING
questions.direct_answer: For a grouped query the **logical order** is FROM → WHERE → **GROUP BY** → **HAVING** → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. WHERE filters rows *before* grouping, HAVING filters groups *after*, and SELECT (with its aliases) is computed near the end.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know where GROUP BY/HAVING sit in execution order.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking HAVING runs before grouping or that SELECT aliases work in WHERE.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Tie the order to why aggregates need HAVING and aliases fail in WHERE.

sections.title: Execution Order for GROUP BY Queries
sections.content:
A grouped query runs in this **logical order**: `FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT`. First the table is read, then `WHERE` filters individual rows, then `GROUP BY` forms buckets, then `HAVING` filters those buckets using aggregates, and only then does `SELECT` compute the output columns.

This order explains the rules: aggregates live in HAVING (groups exist by then), and SELECT aliases can't be used in WHERE (SELECT hasn't run yet) but can be used in ORDER BY.

sections.title: Grouped Query Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[FROM
read table] --> B[WHERE
filter rows] B --> C[GROUP BY
form groups] C --> D[HAVING
filter groups w/ aggregates] D --> E[SELECT
compute columns + aliases] E --> F[ORDER BY
sort, aliases OK] F --> G[LIMIT
cap rows] ```

sections.title: Each clause in its place
sections.content:
```sql
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount   -- 5: compute output
FROM employees                              -- 1: read
WHERE active = true                         -- 2: filter rows
GROUP BY department                         -- 3: form groups
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5                          -- 4: filter groups
ORDER BY headcount DESC                      -- 6: sort (alias OK)
LIMIT 10;                                    -- 7: cap
```

Sample output:

| department | headcount |
|---|---|
| Tech | 12 |
| Sales | 7 |

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **HAVING before grouping**: HAVING runs *after* GROUP BY — it needs the groups to exist.
- **Alias in WHERE**: WHERE runs before SELECT computes the alias.
- **Aggregate in WHERE**: no groups yet — use HAVING.
- **Filtering rows in HAVING**: slower; do row filters in WHERE.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Order**: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.
- **WHERE** filters rows before grouping.
- **HAVING** filters groups after grouping.
- **SELECT** (and aliases) computed late — usable in ORDER BY only.
- **Aggregates** are valid from HAVING onward.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: In a grouped query the clauses execute in a fixed logical order: FROM first, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then SELECT, then ORDER BY, and finally LIMIT. So the database reads the table, WHERE filters the individual rows, GROUP BY collects them into buckets, HAVING filters those buckets using aggregate conditions, and only then does SELECT compute the output columns and aliases. Understanding this single sequence answers most of the confusing questions about grouped queries. Why do aggregate conditions have to go in HAVING and not WHERE? Because WHERE runs before grouping, so at that point there are no groups and no counts to test, whereas by the time HAVING runs the groups exist. Why can't you use a column alias from SELECT inside WHERE? Because SELECT runs after WHERE, so the alias doesn't exist yet; but you can use that alias in ORDER BY, which runs after SELECT. And there's a performance takeaway too: always filter individual rows in WHERE rather than HAVING, because WHERE runs earlier and shrinks the data before grouping, so the database has fewer rows to bucket. So if I can remember just one thing, it's this order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.

followup_questions: Why does HAVING run after GROUP BY?
Can you use a SELECT alias in HAVING?
Why is filtering in WHERE faster than HAVING?

questions.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in terms of performance?
questions.title: WHERE vs HAVING Performance in SQL
questions.direct_answer: **WHERE is faster** for non-aggregate filters because it runs *before* `GROUP BY`, shrinking the row set so fewer rows get grouped and aggregated. **HAVING** runs *after* grouping, so it does the full grouping work first, then discards groups — wasted effort when the condition could have been a row filter.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the performance reason to filter in WHERE before grouping.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Doing row-level filtering in HAVING, making the database group rows it will throw away.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Say: filter early, aggregate late — only aggregate conditions justify HAVING.

sections.title: WHERE vs HAVING: Performance
sections.content:
Both can filter, but they run at different stages, and that drives performance. **`WHERE`** filters rows **before** `GROUP BY`, so the database groups and aggregates *fewer* rows. **`HAVING`** filters **after** grouping, so the database does *all* the grouping work and then throws some groups away.

The principle is **filter early, aggregate late**: push every non-aggregate condition into WHERE; reserve HAVING for conditions that genuinely depend on an aggregate.

sections.title: WHERE vs HAVING Performance
sections.content:
emerald|WHERE|~filter early|runs before GROUP BY|fewer rows to group|index-friendly
rose|HAVING|~filter late|runs after GROUP BY|groups then discards|wasted work for row filters
blue|Principle|~filter early aggregate late|push row filters to WHERE|HAVING only for aggregates|
amber|Result|~same answer|but different cost|WHERE usually cheaper|measure with EXPLAIN

sections.title: Performance Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | WHERE | HAVING |
|---|---|---|
| Runs | before GROUP BY | after GROUP BY |
| Rows grouped | fewer (filtered) | all, then discarded |
| Index use | possible | not on the filter |
| Best for | row conditions | aggregate conditions |

sections.title: Slow: row filter done in HAVING
sections.content:
```sql
-- groups EVERY department, then drops 'inactive' ones
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS c
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING department <> 'CONTRACT';   -- row condition in the wrong place
```

sections.title: Fast: row filter in WHERE
sections.content:
```sql
-- excludes rows BEFORE grouping -> fewer rows to group
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS c
FROM employees
WHERE department <> 'CONTRACT'      -- filter early
GROUP BY department;
```

*Same result, but the WHERE version groups fewer rows and can use an index on `department`.*

sections.title: When to Use Which
sections.content:
Use **WHERE** for any condition on a raw column (status, date, id) — it filters before grouping and can use indexes.

Use **HAVING** only when the filter depends on an aggregate (`COUNT(*) > 5`, `SUM(total) > 10000`). If a condition can be expressed without an aggregate, it belongs in WHERE.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **WHERE** filters before grouping — fewer rows to aggregate.
- **HAVING** filters after grouping — groups then discards.
- **Filter early, aggregate late.**
- **Row conditions → WHERE**, aggregate conditions → HAVING.
- **WHERE can use indexes**; the HAVING filter cannot.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: WHERE and HAVING can both filter, but for non-aggregate conditions WHERE is faster, and the reason is purely about when each one runs. WHERE executes before GROUP BY, so it removes rows before any grouping happens, which means the database has fewer rows to bucket and aggregate. HAVING executes after grouping, so the database does the full work of forming every group and computing every aggregate, and only then throws some groups away. If the condition you're applying is really a row-level condition, like excluding contract employees, doing it in HAVING means you grouped a bunch of rows you were always going to discard, which is wasted effort. The principle I keep in mind is filter early, aggregate late. Push every non-aggregate condition into WHERE, because it runs earlier and can often use an index on that column, and reserve HAVING strictly for conditions that genuinely depend on an aggregate, like count greater than five or sum greater than ten thousand. Both approaches return the same answer, so it's easy to write the slow version by accident, but on a large table the difference can be significant, and you can confirm it with EXPLAIN. So my rule is simple: if a condition can be written without an aggregate function, it belongs in WHERE.

beats.content: WHERE runs before GROUP BY and reduces the number of rows the database has to group. HAVING runs after grouping on the already-aggregated results. If your table has one million rows and your condition cuts it to ten thousand, putting that condition in WHERE means GROUP BY only processes ten thousand rows. Putting the same condition in HAVING means the database still groups all one million rows first.
The practical rule: any condition that does not involve an aggregate function belongs in WHERE. Only conditions that reference COUNT, SUM, AVG, or similar aggregates must go in HAVING.

WHERE can also use indexes; HAVING operates on already-processed grouped data

questions.question: Write a SQL query to find departments with more than 3 employees earning above 50000.
questions.title: SQL Query — WHERE + GROUP BY + HAVING Combined
questions.direct_answer: You combine **WHERE** (row filter), **GROUP BY** (bucket by department), and **HAVING** (group filter on a count). To find departments with more than 3 employees earning above 50000: filter `salary > 50000` in WHERE, group by department, then keep groups with `COUNT(*) > 3` in HAVING.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can correctly place a row filter in WHERE and a count filter in HAVING.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting the salary filter in HAVING or the COUNT condition in WHERE.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why salary>50000 must be in WHERE (per-row) and COUNT>3 in HAVING (per-group).

sections.title: Building the Query Step by Step
sections.content:
The question has two filters of *different kinds*. *Earning above 50000* is a **per-row** condition — it belongs in **`WHERE`**, so only high earners are grouped. *More than 3 employees* is a **per-group** condition on a count — it belongs in **`HAVING`**, after `GROUP BY department` forms the buckets.

Getting the placement right is the whole point: row conditions in WHERE, aggregate conditions in HAVING.

sections.title: Query Plan at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|WHERE|~per-row filter|salary > 50000|keep high earners|runs before grouping
blue|GROUP BY|~bucket rows|by department|one group each|enables COUNT
amber|HAVING|~per-group filter|COUNT(*) > 3|keep big groups|runs after grouping
rose|Trap|~swap them|salary in HAVING = wrong|COUNT in WHERE = error|placement matters

sections.title: The complete query
sections.content:
```sql
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS high_earners
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 50000        -- per-row: only high earners enter the groups
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3         -- per-group: keep departments with > 3 of them
ORDER BY high_earners DESC;
```

Sample output:

| department | high_earners |
|---|---|
| Engineering | 7 |
| Sales | 4 |

*Only departments where more than three employees earn above 50000.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Salary filter in HAVING**: `HAVING salary > 50000` is wrong — salary is per-row, not an aggregate.
- **COUNT in WHERE**: `WHERE COUNT(*) > 3` is illegal — no groups exist yet.
- **Counting everyone**: forgetting the WHERE means you count all employees, not just high earners.
- **No ORDER BY**: output order is undefined without it.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`salary > 50000`** is per-row → WHERE.
- **`COUNT(*) > 3`** is per-group → HAVING.
- **GROUP BY department** forms the buckets between them.
- **WHERE runs first**, so only high earners are grouped.
- **Wrong placement** gives wrong results or an error.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: This is a classic interview query because it forces you to place two different kinds of filters correctly. The condition earning above fifty thousand is a per-row condition: it's about each individual employee's salary, so it belongs in WHERE. The condition more than three employees is a per-group condition: it's a count over a department, so it belongs in HAVING, which runs after the grouping. So I'd write SELECT department, COUNT star FROM employees, then WHERE salary greater than fifty thousand to keep only the high earners, then GROUP BY department to bucket them, then HAVING COUNT star greater than three to keep only departments where more than three of those high earners exist, and I'd usually finish with ORDER BY on the count descending. The reason the order matters is that WHERE runs before grouping, so only high earners ever enter the groups, and then the count inside each group is a count of high earners specifically. If you mistakenly put the salary condition in HAVING it's just wrong, because salary isn't an aggregate, and if you put the count condition in WHERE the query errors out because there are no groups yet. So the takeaway is row condition to WHERE, aggregate condition to HAVING.

followup_questions: Why does salary > 50000 go in WHERE and not HAVING?

speakable_v2.hook: Two filters, two homes: salary above 50k is a row filter for WHERE, more-than-three is a group filter for HAVING — swap them and it breaks.

beats.content: Break the problem into two separate conditions: filtering individual employees by salary, and then filtering departments by headcount. The salary condition is a row-level filter — it belongs in WHERE. The headcount condition requires counting after grouping — it belongs in HAVING.

The query structure is: WHERE salary is greater than 50000 cuts down to high earners first. GROUP BY department groups those employees. HAVING COUNT star greater than 3 then keeps only departments where more than 3 of those high earners work.

content: You cannot put the salary condition in HAVING — it is not an aggregate condition
You cannot put the COUNT condition in WHERE — COUNT has not been computed at that stage
Including ORDER BY high_earners DESC at the end ranks departments by size

speakable_v2.cap: Row-level filters go in WHERE, aggregate filters go in HAVING — split the conditions and the query writes itself.
